questions.question: How does Python resolve a variable name?
questions.title: Python's LEGB Name Resolution Rule
questions.direct_answer: For most function code, Python looks for a referenced name in Local, Enclosing-function, Global, then Built-in scope. Assignment inside a function normally makes that name local.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand name lookup, nested functions, shadowing, and why reads and assignments can behave differently.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating LEGB as a runtime search for every assigned name and missing that a binding operation makes the name local to the block.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate lookup from rebinding and explain where `nonlocal` and `global` redirect a binding.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Trace a name from a line of function code to the binding Python will use, including the effect of an assignment in that function.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: LEGB means Local, Enclosing-function, Global, and Built-in scope.
A reference uses the nearest matching binding that is visible from the current code.
Binding a name anywhere in a function normally makes it local throughout that function block.
`nonlocal` rebinds an existing name in the nearest enclosing function scope.
`global` makes bindings in that block target the module's global namespace.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python resolves a name by looking in increasingly wider namespaces. In ordinary function code, the useful memory rule is LEGB: Local, Enclosing-function, Global, and Built-in. The first visible binding found is the one the expression uses.

Local scope belongs to the current function call. Enclosing scopes belong to any lexically surrounding functions. Global means the namespace of the current module, not every module in the application. Built-in scope contains names such as `len` and `print`.

For example, if a nested function reads `tax_rate` and does not bind that name locally, Python can find `tax_rate` in the outer function. That retained connection to an enclosing binding is part of how closures work.

Assignment changes the analysis. If a function binds `count` anywhere in its body, Python normally treats `count` as local in that entire block. Reading it before the local value is assigned raises `UnboundLocalError`; Python does not fall back to a global value with the same name.

`nonlocal count` says that assignments should use an existing binding in the nearest enclosing function scope. `global count` says that assignments should use the module-level binding. Neither keyword is needed merely to mutate an object reached through a visible name, such as appending to a global list, although hidden shared state is often poor design. In production code I prefer parameters, return values, and object attributes because they make data flow explicit. LEGB explains what Python will do; it does not mean reaching into wider scopes is always the clearest design.

sections.title: Namespaces hold bindings
sections.content:
A namespace maps names to objects, and a scope is the region where a namespace can be used without qualification. Calling a function creates a local namespace for that call. A nested function can refer to bindings in still-active enclosing function scopes, even after the outer call has returned, because the closure retains what it needs.

Name resolution follows lexical structure: where the code was defined matters. It does not search through whichever function happened to call it. Module globals are also module-specific; importing a name from another module creates or accesses a binding according to the import statement rather than forming one universal global dictionary.

Built-in names are the final fallback. Assigning `list = []` locally or globally shadows the built-in `list`, which is valid but often confusing.

sections.title: The lookup path
Where each binding lives
sections.content:
| Scope | Created by | Typical lifetime | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local | Current function call | That call | Parameter or local assignment |
| Enclosing | Lexically outer function | Retained if a closure needs it | Counter state |
| Global | Module | Module lifetime | Module constant |
| Built-in | Python runtime | Interpreter lifetime | `len`, `print` |

sections.title: Trace one name through three scopes
sections.content:
```python
label = "global"

def outer():
    label = "enclosing"

    def read_label():
        local_note = "local"
        return local_note, label, len(label)

    return read_label

reader = outer()
print(reader()) # ('local', 'enclosing', 9)
```

`local_note` is local, `label` comes from the enclosing function, and `len` comes from built-ins. The global `label` is shadowed by the nearer enclosing binding.

sections.title: Predict before running
sections.content: If `read_label` adds the line `label = "local"`, its return uses that local binding. If it instead declares `nonlocal label` and assigns to it, the closure changes the binding created by `outer`.

followup_questions: Why can reading a name before a later assignment raise `UnboundLocalError`?
What information does a Python closure retain?

questions.question: When should you use local, nonlocal, and global variables in Python?
questions.title: Local, nonlocal, and global in Python
questions.direct_answer: Use local variables by default. Use `nonlocal` for small state intentionally owned by an enclosing function, and reserve `global` for rare module-level rebinding when explicit parameters or objects are less suitable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can choose a scope that makes ownership and lifetime clear.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `global` as a shortcut for sharing state, which hides dependencies and complicates testing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that mutation of a visible object and rebinding its name are different operations.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Choose the narrowest scope that matches who owns a value, how long it lives, and who is allowed to rebind it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Prefer local variables, parameters, and return values because their data flow is visible.
Use `nonlocal` only to rebind an existing name in a surrounding function scope.
Use `global` only to rebind a name in the current module's global namespace.
Mutating a referenced object does not require `nonlocal` or `global`; rebinding the name does.
For substantial shared state, prefer an object with named state over closure or module globals.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I use local variables for temporary values owned by one function call. Parameters bring dependencies in, and return values send results out, so local data is easy to reason about and each call can be tested independently. This is the default choice.

I use `nonlocal` when a nested function deliberately manages a small piece of state created by an enclosing function. A counter factory is a clear example: the outer call creates `count`, and each call to the returned inner function rebinds that same enclosed count. The name must already exist in an enclosing, non-global scope.

I use `global` much less often. It redirects bindings in the current block to the current module's global namespace. It may be acceptable for tightly controlled module initialization or a very small module-level setting, but frequently changing global state creates hidden dependencies between callers and tests.

Rebinding and mutation are different. If a visible name refers to a list, `items.append(x)` mutates that list and does not rebind `items`, so no scope declaration is required. Writing `items = items + [x]` binds the name and follows the normal local, `nonlocal`, or `global` rules.

For example, a closure-based request ID generator can reasonably use `nonlocal` for one private integer. A shared application cache with eviction rules and metrics deserves a class or dedicated component rather than several functions changing a module dictionary. My decision follows ownership and lifetime: local for one call, an enclosing closure for small private function state, and an explicit object for larger shared state. `global` is a language tool, but it is rarely the best architecture.

sections.title: Scope is an ownership decision
sections.content:
The narrowest useful scope reduces the number of places that can affect a value. Locals belong to one call and naturally disappear when the call ends unless something retains them. Enclosed bindings can survive through a closure, which makes them useful for small private state. Module globals live for the module's lifetime and can be reached from many call paths.

`nonlocal` and `global` are declarations about binding operations in an entire block. They do not create a new namespace, and `nonlocal` cannot invent a missing enclosing binding. Both should appear before uses or assignments that would conflict with the declaration.

When state gains multiple fields, validation rules, or concurrency concerns, an object usually communicates the contract better than widening scope.

sections.title: Pick the state owner
Binding choices
sections.content:
| Choice | Binding target | Good fit | Main cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local | Current function | Per-call calculation | Must pass or return data |
| `nonlocal` | Existing enclosing function binding | Small closure state | Hidden if the closure grows complex |
| `global` | Current module namespace | Rare module-level rebinding | Broad coupling and test interference |
| Object attribute | Explicit object | Rich shared state and behavior | More structure to define |

sections.title: A focused use of nonlocal
sections.content:
```python
def make_id_generator(prefix):
    number = 0

    def next_id():
        nonlocal number
        number += 1
        return f"{prefix}-{number}"

    return next_id

next_order_id = make_id_generator("order")
print(next_order_id()) # order-1
print(next_order_id()) # order-2
```

The state belongs only to this generator. If it later needs persistence, synchronization, or several operations, moving it into a class would make those responsibilities clearer.

followup_questions: What is the difference between mutating an object and rebinding its name?
Why must a `nonlocal` binding already exist?
When should closure state be replaced with a class?

questions.question: Why do Python functions created in a loop often use the loop's final value?
questions.title: Late Binding in Python Closures
questions.direct_answer: Closures capture a binding, not a frozen copy of its current value. When the functions run later, they look up that binding, which contains the loop's final value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand late binding in closures and can deliberately freeze a per-iteration value.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting each lambda to remember the loop value that existed when the lambda was created.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both a default-argument fix and a helper-factory fix, then explain their different storage locations.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Follow the captured name from function creation to later execution and choose an explicit way to retain each iteration's value.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A closure keeps access to an enclosing binding; it does not automatically snapshot its value.
Functions created in one loop usually refer to the same loop-variable binding.
The lookup happens when the function is called, after the loop may have finished.
Use a default parameter such as `lambda value=value: value` to bind the current value.
A helper factory can create a fresh enclosing binding for each function.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python closures use late binding for free variables. The inner function keeps access to an enclosing name, and the value of that name is resolved when the inner function is called rather than copied when the function object is created.

In a loop, each created function usually closes over the same loop-variable binding. The loop repeatedly rebinds that one name. By the time the stored functions run, the loop has finished and the shared binding holds its final value.

For example, `[lambda: number for number in range(3)]` produces three functions, but calling them afterward gives `2, 2, 2`. There are three function objects, yet their free-variable lookup reaches the same final `number`.

One fix is to bind the current value as a default argument: `lambda number=number: number`. Default arguments are evaluated when each lambda is created, so each function stores a different default value. That parameter is local when the lambda runs.

Another fix is a helper factory such as `make_reader(number)` that defines and returns an inner function. Every call creates a fresh enclosing scope and therefore a distinct binding. The factory form is often clearer when more than one value or more logic must be retained. This behavior is not a lambda-only bug; a nested `def` inside the loop follows the same closure rule. I use late binding intentionally when all callbacks should observe the latest shared value, and early binding when each callback represents one historical iteration.

sections.title: The closure keeps a cell, not a snapshot
sections.content:
When an inner function refers to a name from an enclosing function, Python can store that binding in a closure cell. Multiple inner functions may refer to the same cell. Rebinding the enclosing name changes what a later lookup sees.

The common loop surprise has two different times: function objects are created during the loop, but the free name is read during each later call. Nothing asks Python to remember the earlier values.

Early-binding techniques create a new storage location. A default argument stores a value in the function's defaults and exposes it as a local parameter. A factory call creates another enclosing scope with its own binding.

sections.title: Creation time and call time
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Loop
  participant Cell as shared number binding
  participant F as stored functions
  Loop->>Cell: number = 0; create function
  Loop->>Cell: number = 1; create function
  Loop->>Cell: number = 2; create function
  F->>Cell: call first function; read 2
  F->>Cell: call second function; read 2
  F->>Cell: call third function; read 2
```

sections.title: Ways to control the captured value
sections.content:
| Form | What later calls read | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `lambda: value` | Latest enclosing binding | Latest state is intentional |
| `lambda value=value: value` | Creation-time default | One simple value per callback |
| Helper factory | Fresh enclosing binding per call | Several values or clearer named logic |
| `functools.partial` | Stored positional/keyword arguments | Adapting an existing callable |

sections.title: Compare late and early binding
sections.content:
```python
late = [lambda: number for number in range(3)]
early = [lambda number=number: number for number in range(3)]

def make_reader(value):
    def read():
        return value
    return read

factory = [make_reader(number) for number in range(3)]

print([fn() for fn in late])    # [2, 2, 2]
print([fn() for fn in early])   # [0, 1, 2]
print([fn() for fn in factory]) # [0, 1, 2]
```

sections.title: Choose from the meaning
sections.content: A set of UI buttons labelled with the value from each loop iteration needs early binding. A status callback that should always read the newest shared configuration may deliberately use late binding.

followup_questions: Are Python closures late-bound only when written as lambdas?
Why does a default argument freeze the current loop value?
When is late binding useful rather than accidental?

questions.question: What is the difference between positional, keyword, *args, and **kwargs parameters in Python?
questions.title: Python Function Parameter Kinds
questions.direct_answer: Positional parameters receive arguments by position, keyword parameters by name, `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can read and design a Python function signature precisely.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `*args` and `**kwargs` as the only parameter kinds or using them where an explicit contract would be clearer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Include positional-only and keyword-only boundaries and distinguish parameters in a definition from arguments in a call.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Read a signature from left to right and know which calls are accepted, rejected, or collected.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Parameters before `/` are positional-only; callers cannot use their names.
Normal parameters can receive positional or keyword arguments unless another marker restricts them.
`*args` gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple.
Parameters after `*` or `*args` are keyword-only.
`**kwargs` gathers extra keyword arguments into a dictionary; explicit parameters are clearer for a stable API.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A parameter is a name in the function definition, while an argument is a value supplied by a call. A normal parameter can usually be filled by position or by keyword. For example, `connect("db.local", timeout=5)` supplies one positional and one keyword argument.

Parameters placed before `/` are positional-only. Their names are implementation details for callers, which can be useful for built-in-style APIs or when a name might later appear in `**kwargs`. Parameters between `/` and `*` are positional-or-keyword.

`*args` collects any remaining positional arguments into a tuple. It is useful for forwarding calls or for a genuinely variable number of similar values, but it should not hide several unrelated required inputs. The identifier can have another name; the leading star creates the behavior.

A bare `*`, or the end of a `*args` parameter, starts keyword-only parameters. Keyword-only arguments make call sites clearer for options such as `timeout`, `retry`, or `dry_run`, and they prevent a long list of hard-to-read positional values.

`**kwargs` collects unmatched keyword arguments into a dictionary. It helps decorators and adapters forward extensible options, but a public function with a stable contract is usually easier to understand, document, type-check, and validate when important parameters are explicit. For a signature like `def request(url, /, method="GET", *headers, timeout=5, **options)`, `url` is positional-only, `method` is positional-or-keyword, `headers` receives extra positional values, `timeout` is keyword-only, and `options` receives remaining keywords. The signature itself defines the call contract.

sections.title: A signature is an input grammar
sections.content:
Python binds call arguments to parameters before the function body runs. The `/` and `*` markers divide a signature into zones. A binding error, such as a missing required argument, an unexpected keyword, or multiple values for one parameter, raises `TypeError` before normal body logic proceeds.

Variadic parameters are containers: `args` is a tuple and `kwargs` is a dictionary. The reverse forms appear at a call site: `fn(*values)` unpacks an iterable as positional arguments and `fn(**mapping)` unpacks string-keyed entries as keyword arguments.

Good API design exposes meaningful required inputs and uses flexible collection only where flexibility is part of the contract.

sections.title: Read a signature left to right
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[before /: positional-only] --> N[normal: positional or keyword]
  N --> A[*args: extra positional tuple]
  A --> K[after *: keyword-only]
  K --> W[**kwargs: extra keyword dict]
```

sections.title: Parameter kinds at a glance
sections.content:
| Parameter form | Accepted call style | Value inside function |
|---|---|---|
| Before `/` | Position only | One bound object |
| Normal name | Position or keyword | One bound object |
| `*args` | Extra positional values | Tuple |
| After `*` | Keyword only | One bound object |
| `**kwargs` | Extra named values | Dictionary |

sections.title: Exercise every parameter zone
sections.content:
```python
def request(url, /, method="GET", *headers, timeout=5, **options):
    return {
        "url": url,
        "method": method,
        "headers": headers,
        "timeout": timeout,
        "options": options,
    }

result = request(
    "/users",
    "POST",
    "Accept: application/json",
    timeout=10,
    trace=True,
)
print(result)
```

Calling `request(url="/users")` fails because `url` is positional-only. Passing `timeout` positionally after the header values would not fill `timeout`; keyword-only means its name is required at the call site.

sections.title: Design a readable call
sections.content: For `resize(image, width, height, preserve_ratio=True)`, making `preserve_ratio` keyword-only prevents calls such as `resize(photo, 800, 600, False)` whose final meaning is hard to see.

followup_questions: What do `/` and `*` mean inside a Python function signature?
What is the difference between `fn(*values)` and `fn(**values)` at a call site?
When do `*args` and `**kwargs` make an API harder to understand?

questions.question: Why does Python raise UnboundLocalError, and how do you fix it?
questions.title: Understanding Python UnboundLocalError
questions.direct_answer: `UnboundLocalError` occurs when a function tries to read a local name before that local name has a value. Fix the data flow, or deliberately use `nonlocal` or `global` for the intended outer binding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that scope classification comes from bindings in the whole function block.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Python will read a global value before a later local assignment on another branch.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Inspect all binding forms and prefer an explicit parameter-and-return repair when outer state is not truly required.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Explain the error from Python's local-binding rule, then select a repair from the intended owner of the value.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A binding operation anywhere in a function normally classifies that name as local to the block.
Reading the local name before a value has been bound raises `UnboundLocalError`.
Conditional assignment can leave a local unbound on some execution paths.
Prefer initializing the local, passing a parameter, or returning a value when that matches ownership.
Use `nonlocal` or `global` only when rebinding an enclosing or module-level name is deliberate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`UnboundLocalError` is a `NameError` subclass raised when Python tries to read a local variable before a value has been bound to it. The key point is how Python decided that the name was local.

If a function contains an assignment or another binding operation for a name, that name is normally local throughout the function block unless declared `global` or `nonlocal`. Python does not first read a same-named global and then switch to the local after the assignment.

For example, with a global `count = 10`, a function containing `count += 1` fails. Augmented assignment needs to read the current local `count` before writing the new local value, but no local value exists yet. The global binding is shadowed by the function's local classification.

The same error can appear when only one branch initializes a local. If `message` is assigned inside `if error:` and returned after the condition, the false path reaches `return message` without ever binding it. I inspect every path and all binding forms, including loop targets, imports, exception targets, and assignments.

The repair comes from the intended owner. I can initialize a local before the branches, accept the value as a parameter and return the updated result, use `nonlocal` for real closure state, or use `global` for intentional module-level rebinding. Adding a scope keyword without an ownership reason only hides the design problem. I finish with tests for each control-flow path. That proves the name is always bound before it is read and that the selected scope contains exactly the state the function is meant to change.

sections.title: Why a later assignment affects an earlier line
sections.content:
Python determines a function's local names from the block's binding operations. That decision applies to the block, not only to lines after an assignment. At runtime, loading a classified local before its slot contains a value produces `UnboundLocalError`.

Augmented assignment is especially revealing because `total += amount` is both a read and a binding. A plain mutation such as `items.append(value)` reads `items` but does not rebind that name. The former may need a scope declaration or explicit value flow; the latter can reach a visible outer list, though mutating hidden shared state may still be undesirable.

Conditional flow is the other common source. Draw every path to the read and verify that each one passes through a binding.

sections.title: Trace the error
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  E[UnboundLocalError] --> B{Does this function bind the name?}
  B -- Yes --> P{Can execution read it first?}
  P -- Yes --> O[Decide the intended owner]
  O --> L[Initialize/pass/return local value]
  O --> N[Use nonlocal for enclosing state]
  O --> G[Use global for module rebinding]
  P -- No --> X[Inspect another execution path]
```

sections.title: Repair by ownership
sections.content:
| Intended value | Repair | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Per-call result | Initialize a local on every path | Keeps calls independent |
| Input updated by calculation | Parameter + return value | Makes data flow visible |
| Private closure counter | `nonlocal` | Rebinds existing enclosing state |
| True module configuration | `global` with care | Rebinds module namespace |

sections.title: Replace hidden rebinding with explicit flow
sections.content:
```python
count = 10

def broken_increment():
    try:
        count += 1
        return count
    except UnboundLocalError as error:
        return type(error).__name__

def increment(value):
    return value + 1

print(broken_increment()) # UnboundLocalError
count = increment(count)
print(count)              # 11
```

The second form makes the input and new result explicit. If a nested counter intentionally owns the state, `nonlocal` would express a different and valid contract.

sections.title: Check every path
sections.content: In `if found: result = item; return result`, the false path reads an unbound local. Decide whether the function should return `None`, raise an exception, or initialize another explicit result; do not merely silence the error.

followup_questions: Why does `count += 1` both read and bind `count`?
Which binding operations besides assignment can make a name local?
